newsitem.title: GERMANY: France's Canal Plus seen cutting German stakes.
newsitem.headline: France's Canal Plus seen cutting German stakes.

text.p: The French pay television group Canal Plus is planning to reduce or even give up its stakes in Germany's pay TV channel Premiere and the commercial channel Vox, the weekly news magazine Focus said on Sunday.

Such a move could spark a major shake-up of Germany's fledgling pay television market, which has been marked recently by a fierce row between Premiere's German shareholders Bertelsmann and Bavarian mogul Leo Kirch.

The news magazine, in an unsourced article, said Kirch was prepared to take over the 37.5 percent stake in Premiere owned by Canal Plus. Kirch currently holds 25 percent of Premiere and Bertelsmann owns the remaining 37.5 percent.
None of the companies was available for comment.

The article said further that Canal Plus was no longer willing to finance losses at commercial network Vox, where it holds 24.9 percent. Other Vox shareholders include Bertelsmann and majority shareholder Rupert Murdoch's News Corp.
If the Premiere shares go up for sale, it could spark a bidding war between Bertelsmann, Kirch and Murdoch.
Premiere managing director Bernd Kundrun, in a recent interview with Reuters, said the company was valued at about $1,000 per subscriber. It has 1.41 million subscribers.
Kirch, although a Premiere shareholder, last year broke off on his own and set up a new company, DF1, which would concentrate on digital pay television services and compete against Premiere.
Digital television transmission allows more channels to be broadcast in CD-like quality and interactive services such as video-on-demand and home-shopping.
BSkyB, the British satellite pay TV broadcaster whose biggest shareholder is News Corp, has signed a letter of intent with Kirch to take a stake of just under 50 percent in DF1.

Murdoch's involvement with DF1 was seen as a way of putting pressure on Bertelsmann and Canal Plus to sell him a stake in Premiere, which is years ahead of DF1 in building up a customer and market base.
Separately, the news magazine Der Spiegel reported that Kirch was seeking Kundrun's dismassal as head of Premiere.
Kirch lawyer Joachim Theye has asked Bertelsmann and Canal Plus to support the move, but both backed Kundrun and rejected Kirch's demands on Friday, the report said.
Kundrun has launched at least three law suits against DF1.
The most recent dealt Kirch a serious setback as a Hamburg court imposed an injunction against DF1 from marketing its services outside of the state of Bavaria.
Kirch lieutenant Gottfried Zmeck has said that Kundrun was acting in the interests of Bertelsmann and Canal Plus against Kirch.
But Kundrun argues that Kirch, who owns one of the world's largest arsenals of films and movie rights, has withheld crucial new programming from Premiere in order to beef up DF1.
As a result, Kundrun has turned to Bertelsmann.

In December, Premiere obtained the rights to live broadcasts of European Champions League soccer from the German TV station RTL, which is owned by Luxembourg-based media giant CLT/Ufa, which in turn is 50 percent owned by Bertelsmann.
